name: John C. Frémont
role: American explorer, military commander, California senator, presidential candidate and Arizona territorial governor
summary: Frémont promoted free labor, small landholders and western development, combining antislavery advocacy with conquest and Indigenous dispossession. His 1864 campaign defended constitutional restraints despite his earlier martial-law command in Missouri.

notes:
Reviewed exploration, Senate proposals, both presidential campaigns, Civil War command, railway promotion and the Arizona governorship. Downloaded the 1856 compilation and searched its full text; its promotional narration is separated from his reproduced words. The two URLs for that work share one source-word budget. Later civil-liberties policy is distinguished from 1861 emergency measures. General equality does not establish black suffrage or specific segregation laws. No policy assigned from formal territorial assent alone, and no historical inferences were needed. All remaining statements checked individually against the evidence remain unknown.

Merged with an independent claude-sonnet-5-5 audit: 1 answers taken from it, 17 agreed, 0 conflicts settled by the integrator.

claude-sonnet-5-5 notes: Independent second pass. Searched his 1856 and 1864 letters, the 1861 Missouri proclamation and letter to Lincoln, the 1854 railroad letter, his 1881 messages and vetoes as Arizona governor, and volume 1 of the Memoirs (expeditions, almost no political positions; the political volume was never published). Senate roll calls 1850-51 (Voteview) were checked but answer no statement beyond a vote. His Senate speeches (Congressional Globe), his 1879 Arizona message and Interior reports could not be obtained in full text, so Indigenous policy, immigration, economy and most government themes stay null. The 1864 platform planks are known from the nominating committee's letter, not the platform text; Frémont approved its principles but not every measure (he named confiscation as one he rejected). Government actions under him are used only where he issued or defended them.
